title: 3-Read Friday #50: Silence, Coaching, and Errors
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 50 lands on classroom routine, coaching wisdom, and the cognitive science of error, three threads that recur across his newsletter. He opens with Dylan Kane's three practical ideas for making silent work more productive, noting wryly that one of the ideas is his own but insisting that isn't why he picked the post. He follows with Sarah Cottinghatt's three lessons learned from coaching teachers, singling out her Chesterton's-fence-style principle of not dismantling a practice you don't yet understand as the one that resonated most with him. He closes with Jonathan Firth's post on errorless learning versus learning from errors, describing his own long-standing obsession with mistakes and misconceptions and crediting Firth's piece with sending him off to do further reading on the question of whether errors are just inevitable or actually desirable.
points: Barton flags his own contribution to Kane's silent-work ideas while explicitly disclaiming that as his reason for selecting the post, a small editorial credibility move.
He singles out Cottinghatt's 'don't dismantle what you don't understand' principle as the single most resonant lesson among her three.
He frames Firth's post as having actively changed his reading list, describing it as sending him off to do further research on errorless learning.
He states a long-running personal fascination with mistakes and misconceptions, framing this issue's third pick as part of an ongoing inquiry rather than a one-off interest.
quotes: Dylan shares three practical ideas to help students work more productively in silence.
